evidence.title: Radiology staff perspectives after decommissioning an artificial intelligence (AI) tool for expedited lung cancer triage
evidence.outcome: Staff perceptions of workflow, patient care and emotional impact after AI decommissioning
evidence.effect: Mixed responses: relief at reduced workflow disruption and emotional burden alongside regret over lost patient benefit; comfort with AI on own imaging fell to 25.6% from 31.1%, 48.3%, 47.2%.
evidence.quote: Decommissioning generated mixed responses, combining operational relief with perceived loss of clinical benefit.

evidence.title: Responsible Artificial Intelligence Off-Boarding in Radiology: Staff Perspectives on Decommissioning and a Proposed Withdrawal Framework
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR
evidence.outcome: Staff-perceived disruption and benefit after decommissioning of chest radiograph AI triage tool
evidence.effect: Perceived patient benefit stable (70% vs 71.1% pre-implementation); logistical burden 35% (14 of 40) post-decommissioning, versus 26.4% late implementation and 51.7% early implementation.
evidence.quote: Decommissioning produces both operational relief and perceived clinical loss, with effects differing by staff role.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether a formal AI decommissioning protocol reduces disruption, data leakage, or lost records, and support for the practice rests on six frameworks and commentaries. Two staff surveys from one UK radiology deployment show that retiring an AI tool produced mixed effects on workflow and staff attitudes.

perspectives.view: No study compares decommissioning with and without a formal protocol. The two available reports are descriptive surveys of 40 UK staff, and they may draw on the same respondents. They describe perceptions after one tool was retired and cannot show that any protocol step works. Certainty about the practice cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

Staff-perceived patient benefit stayed near pre-implementation levels after retirement (70% vs 71.1%), and 35% of respondents reported logistical burden. These figures suggest that retirement carries some disruption. The surveys did not measure missed findings, lost records, or data exposure, so the harms the protocol targets remain unmeasured.

After decommissioning, staff reported relief at reduced workflow disruption alongside regret over lost patient benefit. Comfort with AI on their own imaging fell to 25.6% from earlier values of 31.1%, 48.3%, and 47.2%. This suggests that retirement affects staff attitudes as well as workflow, though no study evaluated transition planning or staff notification.

Reported logistical burden was 35% after decommissioning, compared with 51.7% in early implementation and 26.4% in late implementation. Retirement may therefore create a workload increase smaller than adoption does. No study reports the staff time or cost of running a formal decommissioning protocol.

NIST AI 600-1 states that protocols should allow generative AI systems to be deactivated when necessary, and the governance frameworks list decommissioning as a lifecycle step. None of the supplied sources specifies record-retention periods or notification duties, so health systems will need to map these steps to their own legal obligations.

Both surveys asked staff, not patients, about the effects of retirement. The chatbot equity roadmap asks health systems to identify alternative services so that patient care continues, and the pediatric framework calls for a planned move to a non-AI workflow. No study reports whether patients were told about a retirement or lost access to help.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare AI retirements that used a structured protocol with those that did not, and they should measure care continuity, record completeness, data exposure incidents, patient notification, and staff time, across several sites and tool types.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither hazard survey reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and both surveyed only UK radiology staff. The effects of AI retirement on patients who rely on chatbots or language support, which one endorsing commentary raises, are therefore undocumented.
